tier_reason: The README's 'Performance comparison table' lists Option 1-13 in bits/cycle (Golden 62.00, 16-byte tabular 8.00, 8-byte hardware 21.30, naive 0.09-0.33), and the benchmark code (CRC/main.cpp) plus an MSVC v142 project with Release x64 /O2 /Oi /arch:AVX2 (CRC/CRC.vcxproj) are public. No CPU model is named anywhere, and main.cpp derives 'bits/cycle' from wall-clock ns by assuming a 4 GHz clock, so this is first-party data short of A.

corrections.baseline: The author's own C++/asm reimplementations of bitwise (naive) and slicing-by-1..16 tabular CRC-32C, plus a single-stream SSE4.2 _mm_crc32_u64 loop. zlib is never mentioned or tested.
corrections.workload: CRC-32C (Castagnoli poly 0x82F63B78 reflected, the polynomial hard-wired in the x86 SSE4.2 crc32 instruction) of a 900 KB buffer of mt19937 (seed 5) random bytes, repeated 20-10000 runs per option. It compares 13 implementations from bitwise through 16-byte tabular and 1/8-byte hardware crc32 up to 'Golden': 3 parallel SSE4.2 crc32 streams recombined with a PCLMULQDQ carry-less multiply and a LUT of shift constants. There is also a 2-way AMD Jaguar variant.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Golden: ~62 bits/cycle vs 8.00 bits/cycle for the 16-byte tabular version (7.75x, derived from page data) and vs 21.30 bits/cycle for a plain 8-byte hardware crc32 loop (~2.9x, derived from page data). The page says naive implementations are 'more than 150x slower than our final Golden result' (0.09-0.33 bits/cycle).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: MSVC v142 (Visual Studio 2019), Release x64: /O2 (MaxSpeed), /Oi intrinsics, /arch:AVX2 (per CRC/CRC.vcxproj). The README table does not state which build produced it.
corrections.caveats: This computes CRC-32C (Castagnoli), not the IEEE CRC-32 used by zlib, gzip, PNG and ZIP. The x86 crc32 instruction cannot compute IEEE CRC-32, so it is not a drop-in for zlib crc32(). The README is an educational derivation with a self-reported bits/cycle table on an unnamed 'high-end modern x86 CPU'. main.cpp computes bits/cycle from wall-clock time assuming a 4 GHz clock. The project is a Windows-only MSVC solution and needs SSE4.2 + PCLMULQDQ.

notes: The numbers match the README table exactly and >150x vs naive is stated on the page. The record wrongly framed the baseline as zlib-style CRC32 and the algorithm as 'PCLMULQDQ folding'. It is 3-way crc32-instruction interleaving with a CLMUL recombine, and the polynomial is CRC-32C. Metadata checked: MIT, 352 stars, last commit 2021-04-25, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: The README's BENCHMARKS table (Core i7-12700K, 32GB RAM) states 'CRC32 of 1GB data | 0.2 sec | 1.1 sec | 5.5x' vs miniz 3.0. The repo has only README.txt, LICENSE and stb_zip.h: no benchmark code, compiler or flags, so these are numbers without methodology.

corrections.caveats: The CRC comparison is not like-for-like. stb_crc32 in stb_zip.h uses _mm_crc32_u64 (x86 SSE4.2) or crc32cx (ARM) when available, and those compute CRC-32C (Castagnoli), not the IEEE CRC-32 that ZIP and miniz use. With SSE4.2 enabled, its own extraction CRC check would fail on real ZIP files. Its correct IEEE path is a 256-entry byte-table loop unrolled 8x, the same algorithm as miniz 3.0's mz_crc32 (unrolled 4x), so a real 5.5x win on the same function is not credible. There is no benchmark code. The header also has placeholder 'AES' and a CRC32-based 'PBKDF2/HMAC', which suggests unvetted, possibly generated code.

notes: The README numbers exist but belong to a different checksum. The only fast path computes CRC-32C, which is wrong for ZIP. The IEEE CRC-32 path matches miniz's byte-table algorithm, so the project is not actually faster at the baseline's function. It is also only 8 stars with 4 commits, all on 2025-08-13. Metadata checked: MIT, not a fork, not archived, stale (last commit 2025-08-13).

tier_reason: The README states '20-30x faster than the standard library'. Its chart (from benchmark.py, timeit over os.urandom inputs) plots only Python's base64.b64encode against the project's own scalar/SSSE3/AVX/AVX2/AVX512 encode paths. There is no CPU, compiler or flag detail, so this is first-party C tier.

corrections.claimed_speedup: '20-30x faster than the standard library' (README). The chart shows encode only: e.g. stdlib ~160 us vs AVX2/AVX512 ~4-5 us per call at ~65k-byte inputs (read off the chart). The README line 'Benchmarks faster than any other C base64 library' is not backed by benchmark.py, which compares only against Python stdlib base64.
corrections.caveats: This is a thin Cython wrapper (src/turbob64.pyx) over a vendored, prebuilt powturbo/Turbo-Base64 static library (src/lib/libtb64.a, with powturbo's GPL-3.0 notice). All performance comes from Turbo-Base64. The chart's x-axis reaches ~65k, but the committed benchmark.py loops 10000-50000, so the image came from a different script version. Only encoding is benchmarked. No CPU or compiler is stated. The PyPI package turbob64 was last released as 1.1.1 on 2023-08-07.

notes: This is really the known-list project powturbo/Turbo-Base64 (https://github.com/powturbo/turbo-base64) repackaged as a Python binding with a prebuilt libtb64.a. The binding could at most be mentioned on the Turbo-Base64 entry. Metadata checked: GPL-3.0, 15 stars, last commit 2023-08-07 (abandoned), not a fork, not archived.
